## Games of trust, fairness, and cooperation

These are classic lab games. "Nash" here just means the cold, self-interested prediction—not what people always do.

The **Ultimatum Game** asks one player to offer a split of a pot; the other can accept or reject (rejection zeros both payoffs). Cold theory says accept any positive crumb; real people often reject unfair splits [^1]. The **Trust Game** lets a first mover send money that grows; a second mover decides how much to return [^2]. The **Prisoner's Dilemma** (and its repeated cousins) asks whether to cooperate or defect when mutual cooperation beats mutual defection but temptation to defect is real [^3].

| Game | Cold prediction | Tea / warmth pattern in packs | Alcohol pattern in packs | Anchors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ultimatum | Tiny offers; accept anything above zero | Offers nearer fair **40%–50%** splits | More rejection of unfair offers (≤ about 30%) | Güth et al. (1982); Morewedge et al. (2014) [^1][^4] |
| Prisoner's Dilemma | Both defect | More mutual cooperation | Volatile defection or sloppy play | Axelrod (1984) [^3] |
| Trust Game | Send nothing; return nothing | Higher first sends and more reciprocity | High sends with higher betrayal risk | Berg et al. (1995) [^2] |

Ultimatum: someone offers you a split of $10; if you reject, both get nothing. Cold theory says accept $1; many people reject unfair splits. Trust Game: you send money that grows; the other person decides how much to return. Opening trust is not the same as forever trust.

Snapshots:

| Game | Result | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ultimatum, alcohol ~0.06% BAC (N = 92) | Unfair-offer (≤20%) rejection **82.4%** vs **58.1%** placebo | Morewedge et al. (2014) [^4] |
| Trust Game / fairness, warm ~60°C mug | First-mover investment about **+24.8%** (pack narrative) | Kang et al. (2011) [^5] |
| Iterated Dilemma, warm drink (pack) | Mutual cooperation rounds 1–10: **62.5%** vs **47.2%** control | Inagaki & Eisenberger (2013; pack) [^6] |

Warmth and ritual can lift **opening** trust (about **+15% to +25%** in cited work). If the other side defects in later rounds, cooperation often collapses. Incentives still dominate over a long game—Axelrod's tournaments already taught that cooperation needs structure, not only good vibes [^3].

People sometimes hope: "Serve tea and the negotiation becomes win–win forever." Opening trust is real in cited work; forever cooperation is not. Ritual can also blunt the brain's error-alarm and lower anxiety (Chapter 3)—discussed in the packs alongside fewer hyper-aggressive rejections of unfair offers. Calmer bodies can mean less hair-trigger bargaining—not automatic fairness forever. And remember Chapter 3's replication caution: warmth effects on generosity are smaller and less reliable than early headlines suggested [^7].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: Ultimatum, Trust, and Dilemma snapshots"}
| Game | Cold prediction | Tea / warmth pattern in packs | Alcohol pattern in packs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ultimatum | Tiny offers; accept anything above zero | Offers nearer fair **40%–50%** splits | More rejection of unfair offers (≤ ~30%) |
| Prisoner's Dilemma | Both defect | More mutual cooperation | Volatile defection or sloppy play |
| Trust Game | Send nothing; return nothing | Higher first sends and more reciprocity | High sends with higher betrayal risk |

Anchors: Güth et al. (1982) Ultimatum;[^1] Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe (1995) Trust Game;[^2] Axelrod (1984) cooperation structure.[^3]

Snapshots:

- Ultimatum, alcohol ~0.06% BAC (N = 92): unfair-offer (≤20%) rejection **82.4%** vs **58.1%** placebo.[^4]
- Trust / fairness, warm ~**60°C** mug: first-mover investment about **+24.8%** (pack narrative of Kang).[^5]
- Iterated Dilemma, warm drink (pack): mutual cooperation rounds 1–10 about **62.5%** vs **47.2%** control.[^6]

Warmth and ritual can lift **opening** trust (~**+15% to +25%** in cited work); if the other side defects later, cooperation often collapses. Incentives still dominate over a long game.[^3] Keep Lynott et al.'s failed warmth-gift replication in view when someone sells "serve tea, win the deal."[^7]
:::

[^1]: Güth, W., Schmittberger, R., & Schwarze, B. (1982). An experimental analysis of ultimatum bargaining. *Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 3*(4), 367–388.

[^2]: Berg, J., Dickhaut, J., & McCabe, K. (1995). Trust, reciprocity, and social history. *Games and Economic Behavior, 10*(1), 122–142. https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1995.1027

[^3]: Axelrod, R. (1984). *The Evolution of Cooperation*. Basic Books.

[^4]: Morewedge, C. K., Krishnamurti, T., & Ariely, D. (2014). Focused on fairness: Alcohol intoxication increases the costly rejection of inequitable rewards. *Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 50*, 15–20. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2013.08.006

[^5]: Kang, Y., Williams, L. E., Clark, M. S., Gray, J. R., & Bargh, J. A. (2011). Physical temperature affects response to fairness. *PLOS ONE, 6*(1), e15836. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0015836

[^6]: Inagaki, T. K., & Eisenberger, N. I. (2013). Shared neural mechanisms underlying social warmth and physical warmth. *Psychological Science, 24*(11), 2272–2280.

[^7]: Lynott, D., et al. (2014). Replication of "Experiencing physical warmth promotes interpersonal warmth" by Williams and Bargh (2008). *Social Psychology, 45*(3), 216–222. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000187
